input.query: Mapping Languages and Demographics with Georeferenced Corpora: hypothesis for why Twitter data makes better predictions about the inventory of languages used in each country

output.reason: The evidence does not show the authors offering an explicit hypothesis specifically explaining why Twitter data makes better predictions about the language inventory. However, the Discussion and Population Demographics sections provide related interpretive explanations: Twitter data matches populations better when weighted by GDP (implying Twitter represents wealthier populations, possibly because collection is based on urban areas), Twitter has fewer missing languages, and both English and Spanish are very common on Twitter so countries using these languages are well represented. These are partial explanations, not a single stated hypothesis for the language-inventory result.

claims.text: The paper states that Twitter data makes better predictions about the inventory of languages used in each country.
The authors report that, where ground-truth language-use data is available, Twitter has fewer missing languages (cases where census languages are not found in digital texts).
The authors note that false positives are uncommon overall but occur more in Twitter data, meaning Twitter suggests languages are frequently used in a country when census data does not.

The authors imply that Twitter as a platform represents more wealthy populations than general web-crawled data, based on Twitter matching populations better when weighted by GDP and worse when weighted by internet-usage statistics.
The authors offer an alternate interpretation that their Twitter collection is based on urban areas, which tend to have more wealthy populations.
The authors find that Twitter provides a better representation of North America and Oceania, while the two corpora agree in Europe, parts of Africa with ground-truth data, and South America.
The authors note that English and Spanish are very common on Twitter, so any country predominantly using these two languages will have a good representation by default.
The authors state that many countries have only a few languages, so a high true positive rate for a country could reflect only one or two languages.
The authors report that on Twitter most false positives are in Russia and Eastern Europe, with over-predicted languages also in the US and Canada, South Africa, France, India, and Australia.
The authors state that more research is needed to distinguish between immigration, tourism, and business as alternate sources of false positive languages appearing in digital data sets.

The authors say patterns from Twitter and web-crawled data diverge significantly and that this simply reflects that data drawn from Twitter and web pages will likely represent people from different places.
